newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Physical cocoa buyers return but stg hampers trade.
newsitem.headline: Physical cocoa buyers return but stg hampers trade.

text.p: European buyers of cash cocoa have made scattered bean purchases in the physical market this week, encouraged by a fall in futures prices but a rise in sterling against European currencies has modified buying enthusiasm.

Some traders cited talk of good German demand but others said the latest currency move, taking the pound to a 4-1/2 year peak above 2.80 marks, had discouraged many clients from taking on much needed cover.
"There hase been some German manufacture inquiry but not the mountains of buying you hear about in some quarters," said one continental European trader.

"My view is they're still standing back and hoping the whole thing will go away," another said. "All year they've been looking at a market at 850 stg times 2.60 (sterling/mark rate) and now its 1,020 stg times 2.80 -- it's a huge increase in mark terms and they don't want to chase it.
"At some point, they're going to have to come in," he added.
London-traded futures were around 1,020 stg a tonne, basis benchmark July by the midsession on Friday, down from near 1,055 stg at the same time last week.
On the supply side, traders said the market continued to be supplied with Ivorian cocoa but there was little Ghanaian supply around after small amounts traded earlier in the week.
Ivorian shippers had mostly closed out their long positions, having offered cocoa at prices far below the second hand market.
Dealers quoted nearby Ivorian beans trading around 25 stg under the terminal market, against Ivorian shipper offers which were as low as 35 stg under.

The situation was still very confused in the Ivory Coast, traders said, with some shippers not actually having the cocoa they had promised to sell and having to return to the Caisee to deblock (receive export permit) more cocoa. This had contributed to over-bidding at the Caisse, they said.

The market was still focused on the general level of European cocoa stocks and the size and quality of the upcoming mid-crop, which some said offered the potential for a serious supply shortage over the summer months.
The latest SGS warehouse data show Dutch cocoa stocks in early March near 600,000 tonnes, up 50,000 on a month earlier.

"If you look at the SGS figures, it's easy to believe that Europe is awash with cocoa. But if you look at the available stocks and then factor in the small mid-crop scenario, then you can paint a very bullish picture indeed," one said.

The market believes the Ivorian mid-crop will not only be well short of last year's bumper 200,000 tonnes but may also be plagued by size and quality difficulties, making a sizeable proportion untenderable against the terminal market.

This would play into the hands of U.S. trade house Phibro, thought to be sitting on a large physical position and betting, some believe, on a lucrative combination of tight summer supply and industry customers desperately needing to cover needs.
